This analysis and results are still in an early stage and are considered preliminary. Despite this fact, the results obtained are valuable for understanding the impact of preheating on the stress and distortion of the tank floor. Further research is required, however, to provide a more accurate quantification of these effects. The preheating analysis was conducted by adapting the mechanical portion of the molten salt tank model and using real temperature data to interpolate thermal profiles at every time step for the tank floor, walls, and roof. The thermal profile was interpolated at each time step and used as a boundary condition in the model. The model was configured in ANSYS Workbench, as shown in the flow diagram in Figure 30. Initially, the tank geometry was imported into a static structural analysis to calculate the initial mesh deformation. The deformed mesh is linked to a transient thermal analysis that incorporates preheating data and interpolates temperature measurements across the entire tank mesh. Finally, the deformed mesh and the interpolated preheating conditions are input into a transient structural analysis. This final analysis also integrates the residual stress and plastic strains resulting from the floor welding fabrication model. Figure 30. Flow Diagram of the Preheating Model Implementation in ANSYS Workbench. Nonlinear static and transient structural analyses were conducted on the tank, using a structured mesh of shell elements, as illustrated in Figure 31. A fixed support was applied to the floor's central node. The friction coefficient at the interface between the steel floor and the sand was defined as 0.5. Since the sand's behavior beyond its initial frictional resistance was not of interest, it was represented by a fixed support. 24 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 31. Structured shell meshing for the tank's wall, floor, and roof. One of the main challenges during the preheating analysis was the limited number of temperature data points. Only a few temperature profiles were measured in some locations of the tank wall and floor (spacing between sensors was 3 m in the wall and 6 m in the floor). This dataset associates each measured temperature with its corresponding normalized x, y, and z coordinates within the 39.6 m diameter tank. In this initial model, only one such dataset is used, representing the temperature distribution at the start of preheating on the first day. In the Transient Thermal analysis, the imported preheating temperature dataset was used to interpolate temperature values across all nodes of the heating tank grid. Three interpolation techniques—Triangulation, Distance-Based Average (DBA), and Kriging—were assessed for this purpose, with their results visualized in the isometric views of Figure 32 [16-18].
